title: Why We Sweat
summary: What sweat glands do, how sweating cools the body through evaporation, why heat and exercise make you sweat more, and why drinking water matters.
poll: Sweating is a sign that something is wrong with your body.

versions.title: Why Do We Sweat?
versions.text:
Touch your skin. It may feel wet. That wet stuff is sweat!

Sweat comes from tiny holes in your skin. These holes are called sweat glands. You have them all over your body. Your face has many glands. Your back has many too. Your arms have them under too.

Why do you sweat? Your body makes heat. You make heat when you run. You make heat when you play. Hot weather makes heat too.

Sweat has a job to do. It helps cool you down. Wet drops sit on your skin. Then the air dries them up. This takes heat away.

Sweat is mostly water. When you sweat a lot, you lose water. You must drink water to get it back.

So do not worry when you sweat. It is your body's way to stay cool. Just remember to drink water!

versions.title: Why Do We Sweat?
versions.text:
Touch your skin on a hot day. It may feel wet. That wetness is sweat!

Sweat comes out through tiny holes in your skin. These holes are called sweat glands. You have them all over your body. Your face has many glands. Your back has many too. You have many under your arms as well.

Why does your body make sweat? Your body makes heat all the time. It makes even more heat when you run or play. Hot weather adds extra heat too.

Sweat helps cool your body down. Wet drops sit on top of your skin. Then the air slowly dries them up. This drying takes heat away from your skin.

Sweat is mostly water, with a little salt mixed in. When you sweat a lot, your body loses water. That is why you must drink water to replace it.

So the next time you feel hot, do not worry about sweating. It is simply your body's clever way of staying cool. Just remember to drink enough water!

versions.title: Why We Sweat
versions.text:
On a hot day, or after you run and play hard, your skin may feel wet. This wetness is sweat. It has an important job to do.

Sweat comes out through tiny openings in your skin. These are called sweat glands. The glands are spread across most of your skin. You usually notice sweat most on your face, back, and under your arms.

Why does your body make sweat? Your body always makes a little heat. It makes even more heat when you run, play, or exercise. Hot weather adds extra heat too.

Sweat helps cool your body down. Wet drops sit on top of your skin. Then the air slowly dries them. This drying is called evaporation. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin. That makes you feel cooler.

Sweat is made mostly of water. A small amount of salt is mixed in too. When you sweat a lot, your body loses water that it needs. That is why you must drink water to replace it.

So the next time you feel hot, do not worry about sweating. It is your body's clever way of keeping cool. Just remember to drink enough water.

versions.title: Why We Sweat
versions.text:
On a hot day, or after you run and play hard, you probably notice wet drops on your skin. This wetness is sweat. It has an important job to do for your body.

Sweat is made by tiny openings in your skin. These are called sweat glands. The glands are spread across almost all of your skin. You usually notice sweat most on your face, back, and under your arms, where there are more glands.

Why does your body make sweat? Your body always makes a small amount of heat. It makes even more heat when you run, play, or exercise hard. Hot weather adds extra heat too.

Sweat helps cool your body down. Wet drops sit on top of your skin, and the air slowly dries them. Scientists call this evaporation. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin. That is what makes you feel cooler.

Sweat is made mostly of water, with a small amount of salt. When you sweat a great deal, especially during exercise or on hot days, your body loses water it needs. That is why it matters to drink water before and after you sweat heavily.

So the next time you feel hot, remember that sweating is simply your body's clever way of staying cool.

versions.title: Why We Sweat
versions.text:
Have you ever noticed wet drops on your skin after running hard, or on a hot afternoon? This wetness is sweat. It plays an important role in keeping your body safe.

Sweat is made by tiny structures in your skin called sweat glands. The glands are found across most of your body. They are most active on your face, back, and underarms.

Your body always makes a small amount of heat, just by staying alive. Exercise makes your muscles work hard. This produces much more heat than usual. Hot weather adds even more heat from outside. Your body temperature can rise from both directions at once.

Sweat helps bring your temperature back down. This happens through a process called evaporation. Liquid sweat sits on your skin until the air makes it evaporate. As sweat evaporates, it pulls heat away from your skin. That is what makes you feel cooler.

Sweat is mostly water, with a small amount of salt. Sweating removes water from your body. Staying hydrated matters, especially during exercise or on hot days. Losing too much water without replacing it can leave you feeling tired, dizzy, or thirsty.

Long ago, a physician named Hippocrates noticed that sweating seemed linked to body heat, long before scientists understood sweat glands or evaporation.

versions.title: Why We Sweat

Have you ever noticed wet droplets on your skin after running hard, or on a scorching afternoon? This wetness is sweat. It plays an important role in protecting your body from dangerous overheating.

Sweat is produced by microscopic structures in your skin called sweat glands. The glands are spread across nearly every part of your body. They are especially active on your face, back, and underarms, places with more glands than most.

Your body always makes a modest amount of heat, simply by staying alive. Physical exercise forces your muscles to work much harder. This produces significantly more heat than usual. Hot weather adds even more heat from outside. Your body temperature rises from two directions at once.

Sweat helps restore your temperature to normal. This happens through a process known as evaporation. Liquid sweat rests on your skin until the air causes it to evaporate. As sweat evaporates, it draws heat energy away from your skin. That is precisely what produces that refreshingly cooler feeling afterward on a very hot day.

Sweat consists mostly of water, along with a modest amount of salt. Sweating continuously removes water from your body. Remaining properly and fully hydrated is essential, especially during exercise or on hot days. Losing too much water without replacing it can leave you feeling tired, dizzy, thirsty, or a bit unwell.

Long ago, the physician Hippocrates observed that sweating seemed closely connected to how the body handled heat, long before scientists understood sweat glands or evaporation.

versions.title: Why We Sweat
versions.text:
Have you ever noticed wet droplets on your skin after running hard, or on a scorching afternoon? This wetness is sweat, and it performs an important function in protecting your body from dangerous overheating.

Sweat is produced by microscopic structures embedded in your skin called sweat glands. The glands are distributed across nearly every part of your body, from your scalp down to your toes. They are especially active on your face, back, and underarms, places that contain far more sweat glands than most other areas of the body.

Your body always generates a modest amount of heat, simply by remaining alive. Physical exercise forces your muscles to work considerably harder than usual. This produces significantly more heat than usual. Hot weather contributes even more heat from the surrounding environment. Your body temperature rises from two directions simultaneously.

Sweat helps restore your internal temperature to normal. This happens through a process known as evaporation. Liquid sweat rests upon your skin until the surrounding air causes it to evaporate. As sweat evaporates, it draws heat energy away from your skin. That is precisely what produces that refreshingly cooler feeling afterward on a hot day.

Sweat consists primarily of water, along with a modest amount of salt. Sweating continuously removes water from your body. Remaining properly hydrated is essential, particularly during exercise or on especially hot days. Losing excessive water without adequately replacing it can leave you feeling fatigued, dizzy, or persistently thirsty and uncomfortable.

Long ago, the physician Hippocrates observed that sweating seemed closely connected to how the body regulated heat, long before scientists fully understood sweat glands or the process of evaporation.

versions.title: Why We Sweat: The Body's Cooling System
versions.text:
The human body contains an internal cooling system. Sweating is its most visible and familiar part. When your skin becomes damp during exercise or on a sweltering day, a remarkable process is quietly underway inside your body.

Sweat glands are tiny structures embedded throughout your skin. They produce sweat when your brain detects that your temperature is climbing. A region deep in the brain called the hypothalamus continuously monitors body temperature. It triggers sweating whenever temperature rises above normal. This regulatory process is known as thermoregulation, an essential bodily function. Scientists have carefully studied thermoregulation in people and in many other animals for a very long time.

Physical exercise generates a good deal of heat, since your muscles contract again and again. Hot weather also adds even more heat from the surrounding outside environment. Either situation on its own, or both occurring together, can push your temperature upward quickly. This activates the hypothalamus's cooling response, which quickly sends a signal to your sweat glands.

Sweat cools the body through a process called evaporation. Liquid sweat sitting on your skin absorbs surrounding heat. It slowly turns into water vapor. That heat is carried away from the body. The skin becomes noticeably cooler than before. This evaporative cooling process works quickly and very efficiently, even on the hottest days of summer.

Sweat is made mostly of water, along with some dissolved salts. Prolonged or heavy sweating gradually uses up the body's water supply. Without drinking enough to replace it, this can lead to dehydration. Dehydration is marked by fatigue, dizziness, headache, and weaker physical performance during exercise or hot weather.

Long before the hypothalamus or thermoregulation were understood, the physician Hippocrates observed a link between sweating and body heat. His early insight was later confirmed by modern scientists studying the human body in great detail.

versions.title: Why We Sweat: The Body's Cooling System
versions.text:
The human body contains an elaborate internal cooling system, and perspiration represents its most visible and readily familiar component. This process unfolds quietly inside the body whenever the skin becomes noticeably damp during strenuous physical exertion or on an especially hot, sweltering day.

Sweat glands are microscopic, highly specialized structures embedded throughout the skin. They produce sweat whenever the brain detects that the internal body temperature is gradually rising. A small region located deep within the brain known as the hypothalamus continuously monitors body temperature. It initiates sweating whenever temperature climbs above its normal baseline, a regulatory process termed thermoregulation. Scientists have carefully studied thermoregulation in humans and in a great many other kinds of animals for a very long time, and they continue to learn important new details about it today.

Physical exercise generates a considerable amount of metabolic heat, since the muscles contract repeatedly and without interruption. Elevated ambient temperature also contributes a substantial amount of additional heat from the surrounding outside atmosphere and environment. Either circumstance occurring on its own, or both occurring simultaneously, can elevate internal temperature rather quickly and quite noticeably. This activates the hypothalamus's cooling response, which quickly and efficiently sends a signal out to the many sweat glands located throughout the body.

Sweat cools the body through the process of evaporation. Liquid sweat resting on the outer surface of the skin absorbs surrounding heat and gradually transforms into water vapor. That heat energy is then carried away from the body entirely, leaving the surface of the skin feeling noticeably cooler than it did before. This evaporative cooling process operates quickly and remarkably efficiently, even on the very hottest and most humid days of the entire summer season.

Sweat is composed primarily of plain water, together with dissolved salts and minerals. Prolonged or especially strenuous sweating gradually and steadily depletes the body's entire available water supply. Without drinking enough fluid to replace what is lost, this can precipitate dehydration, a condition characterized by persistent fatigue, severe dizziness, headache, and markedly diminished physical performance during exercise or in hot weather conditions.

Long before the hypothalamus or thermoregulation were scientifically comprehended, the ancient physician Hippocrates observed a connection between perspiration and the body's handling of heat. This early insight was later corroborated by modern scientists studying the human body and its many complex internal systems in considerable detail, many centuries after Hippocrates first wrote about it.

versions.title: Why We Sweat: The Body's Cooling System
versions.text:
The human body contains an elaborate and highly sophisticated internal cooling system, and perspiration constitutes its single most visible and readily familiar component, unfolding quietly inside the body whenever the skin becomes noticeably damp during strenuous physical exertion or on an exceptionally sweltering day.

Sweat glands are microscopic, highly specialized structures embedded extensively throughout the integument, producing sweat whenever the brain detects that the internal body temperature is gradually ascending beyond its usual normal range. A small region located deep within the brain designated the hypothalamus continuously monitors body temperature and initiates sweating whenever that temperature climbs above its normal baseline, a regulatory process termed thermoregulation. Scientists have meticulously studied thermoregulation in humans and in a great many other species of animals for a very long time, and they continue to learn important new details about its mechanisms today.

Physical exertion generates a considerable amount of metabolic heat, since the skeletal muscles contract repeatedly and without any interruption, while elevated ambient temperature simultaneously contributes a substantial amount of additional heat from the surrounding outside atmosphere and environment. Either circumstance occurring on its own, or both occurring simultaneously, can elevate internal temperature rather quickly and quite noticeably, activating the hypothalamus's cooling response, which quickly and efficiently transmits a signal outward to the many sweat glands located throughout the body.

Sweat cools the body through the physical process of evaporation: liquid sweat resting upon the outer surface of the skin absorbs surrounding thermal energy and gradually transforms into water vapor, and that thermal energy is then carried away from the body entirely, leaving the surface of the skin feeling noticeably cooler than it did before. This evaporative cooling process operates quickly and remarkably efficiently, even on the very hottest and most humid days of the entire summer season each year.

Sweat is composed primarily of plain water, together with various dissolved salts and electrolytes, and prolonged or especially strenuous sweating gradually and steadily depletes the body's entire available water reserves. Without drinking an adequate amount of fluid to replace what is lost, this can precipitate dehydration, a condition characterized by persistent fatigue, severe dizziness, headache, and markedly diminished physical and cognitive performance during exercise or in hot weather conditions.

Long before the hypothalamus or thermoregulation were scientifically comprehended, the ancient physician Hippocrates observed a connection between perspiration and the body's overall management of heat, a very early insight that was later corroborated by modern scientists studying the human body and its many complex internal systems in considerable detail, many long centuries after Hippocrates first wrote about it.

HIGH.prompt: Explain, using scientific vocabulary from the article, how the hypothalamus and evaporation work together to keep the body from overheating, and why dehydration is a risk during intense exercise.
checklist: I explained the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation.
I explained how evaporation cools the body.
I explained why dehydration can occur and why it matters.
HIGH.modelAnswer: When the body's internal temperature rises, whether from exercise, hot weather, or both, the hypothalamus detects the change and triggers sweat glands as part of thermoregulation. Liquid sweat then sits on the skin until it evaporates, and evaporation carries heat away from the body, cooling the skin noticeably. However, because sweat is made mostly of water, prolonged or intense sweating steadily depletes the body's water supply. Without replacing that lost fluid, a person risks dehydration, which can cause fatigue, dizziness, and reduced physical performance. This is why staying hydrated is just as important as the cooling process itself.
